extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics and classical numeration systems
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed account of Greek systems for writing numbers, fractions, large numbers, and practical calculation methods (abacus, multiplication) with comparisons to Egyptian/Herodianic/Archimedean systems. Aimed to describe notation conventions and their practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetic numerals scheme (orthodox alphabetic notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthodox alphabetic notation distinguished numerals by a horizontal stroke above each sign or group; specific alphabetic signs used for units (1–9), tens (10–90), hundreds (100–900), thousands (1000–9000). (For printing the horizontal stroke is often omitted.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists of the actual signs for units/tens/hundreds/thousands are given; the horizontal stroke marks numeral use. Examples and the printed omission of the stroke are noted. Use this scheme when writing numbers in the 'alphabetic' Greek system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of Herodianic vs alphabetic numerals (merits/drawbacks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Herodianic (older) numerals correspond closely to Roman numerals (no subtraction notation like IX), while alphabetic numerals use many distinct signs (about twenty-seven) whose values must be memorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cantor criticized alphabetic numerals for requiring more signs and memory; Gow and Cantor regarded them as retrograde for development. Tannery's experimental use found alphabetic notation practically viable. The author argues that users calculate with number-words rather than glyphs and that the only serious drawback of alphabetic numerals is the absence of a zero sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a zero sign (position-value limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek alphabetic numerals lacked a sign for zero in the integral numeral system; a mark used in sexagesimal fractions (ovSev) was not part of the main numeral system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This absence prevents easily expressing an empty denomination in a positional sense. Proposed remedies include showing a blank or special mark in the position (e.g. Diophantus's plan: show a blank or use separators/dots). The text gives examples of how blanks or separators could indicate absent denominations (e.g. 7021 vs 7921).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for large numbers using myriads (M) and dot separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tens of thousands and higher numbers could be written with the letter M (myriad) with the number of myriads above it, or by writing M (or variants) and putting the number of myriads before it separated by a dot from the remaining thousands, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: M = 20000; M/cooe = 71755875 (Aristarchus); Diophantus example: M pv... = 1507984. Powers of myriads could be expressed by repeated M (M, MM...) or by writing the word /xvpLoiSes in full. Use dot separators (following Diophantus) to distinguish myriads groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apollonius' 'tetrads' grouping (groups of four digits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apollonius grouped numbers into tetrads (sets of four digits) meaning 10,000, 10,000^2, 10,000^3, ... and used abbreviations (/x^n, /i^n, etc.) to denote successive powers of 10000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This system abbreviates successive powers of 10000 as special symbols and terms (simple/myriad, double, triple myriads). Example in Pappus: /i jev^^ Kal //^yx Kal /i"^<5-i/ = 5 462 3600 6400 0000. Use tetrads when the decimal-like grouping by 10,000 suits the calculation or textual practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedes' octads (Sand-reckoner system) for very large numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes employed an octad-based scheme: first order runs 1..10^8, the last of first order (10^8) is unit of the second order, and so on; orders are grouped into periods, enabling naming of astronomically large numbers (myriad-myriadth order/period, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The system defines units, orders, and periods recursively (P = 10^8, periods made of 10^8 orders, etc.). It is a tour de force intended to express enormous magnitudes and is distinct from ordinary Greek numeration. Use only when needing to name extremely large numbers in Archimedean context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractions — Egyptian-influenced preference for unit fractions (aliquot parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greeks preferred to express ordinary proper fractions as sums of submultiples (unit fractions), following Egyptian practice; orthodox sign for a submultiple was the letter for the denominator with an accent (e.g. y' = 1/3). Special signs existed for 1/2 and 2/3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When several submultiples are written in sequence, their sum is intended; when following a whole number they add to it. Examples: U' 5' = 1/6 + 1/5 etc.; ambiguous forms could arise when using cardinal numerals followed by accented denominators, so context was important. Later manuscripts sometimes used variant marks (double accents) or Diophantus's alternate forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary Greek fraction notations and ambiguity avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Various forms were used: (a) cardinal numerator + accented-denominator sign (ambiguous), (b) full numerator followed by accented denominator (less ambiguous), (c) transformed ordinal abbreviation with superposed termination, (d) doubled accented letters with numerator in line (Heron), and (e) Diophantus's method (numerator in line, denominator above).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends Diophantus's method as most convenient (numerator below, denominator above), noting that Heron and others used doubled accented letters and sometimes added explicit words like 'fractions' or 'units' for clarity. Beware ambiguous readings where '1 oa' might be misread as 10/1 unless context clarifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diophantus' fractional format (numerator below, denominator above)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diophantus frequently wrote the numerator in the line with the denominator above it (reverse of modern orientation); sometimes the denominator appears to the right like an exponent. He also sometimes writes submultiples using the same stacked arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notation is convenient and often used in Diophantus's problems; editions place a horizontal line between numerator and denominator. Examples: pKa = numerator/121, other Diophantus instances cited. Use this stacked format to avoid ambiguity of accented-denominator-only forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexagesimal fractions (astronomical notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage of base-60 fractions for angles and computations: degrees (360), minutes (60'), seconds (60''), etc.; notation places the integer unit first, then numerals with one accent for first sixtieths (minutes), two accents for seconds, and so on. The symbol O can indicate an empty place (no units of that sixtieth order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel to decimal fractions but base 60; very convenient for astronomical calculation and approximations. Example: /i° /3 = 2° ; /ioipSav n( /i/3' n'' = 47° 42' 40". Ptolemy's Table of Chords example shows accuracy to seventh decimal place when converted. Use O to mark zero in a place when needed (e.g. 0°! 2" 0").

rubrics_metrics.name: Abacus layout and pebble/peg representation (practical calculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek abacus consisted of vertical columns allocated to successive denominations (units, tens, hundreds, thousands, myriads, etc.) with pebbles or buttons indicating counts; each column often divided into a top shorter portion (one button = half the next unit) and a lower portion (several buttons = remainder). Fraction-columns (unciaea 12ths etc.) used different button counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry and borrow operations performed by moving pebbles across columns or by mentally resolving a higher unit into lower units. Top button usually represented 5 units in integer columns; for unciae top represented 6 (½ unit in that system) and five below (total 11 unciae). The Salaminian table and other monuments are discussed as evidence; consider both movable-pebble and fixed-button types when interpreting archaeological boards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical arithmetic methods: Egyptian doubling vs Greek multiplication-table approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Two distinct operational methods: (a) Egyptian doubling — successively double multiplicand and select/add entries corresponding to binary decomposition of multiplier; (b) Greek method — direct use of a multiplication table (tablets preserved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Egyptian method example: to multiply by 13, add 1x + 4x + 8x (doubling chain). The text presents an algorithmic column method (halve multiplier / double multiplicand rows, strike out rows with even first-column entries) illustrated with numerical example. Greeks likely used multiplication tables (a fragment exists on a wax tablet). Choose method according to documentary context: practical arithmetic might employ either technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for complex algebraic or large-number fractions (explicit numerator/denominator wording)
rubrics_metrics.description: When numerator and denominator are algebraic expressions or large numbers, Greeks often wrote the numerator first and separated it by words meaning 'divided by' (e.g., fiopioi, k^ fiopioi) from the denominator: i.e., expressed verbally as numerator divided by denominator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: Mpv .^^'^nS /xopiov k^ . fipfiS = 1507984/262144 (Diophantus IV.28). This verbal separation avoids ambiguity in complex fractional expressions.
